From HolodeckMany of the developers prefer ORMs instead of raw SQL, to interact with their databases. ORMs help us interact with the database in the object-oriented language we prefer. Now let’s see if you are going to build with an ORM, which one of the leading two ORMs in the market for Javascript developers, should be chosen?
You open a new project, run npx prisma init, write a clean schema file, and run prisma db push.
Within five minutes, you have auto-completion for your entire database. You type prisma.user.findMany() and TypeScript gives you autocomplete for every column, relation, and nested object. It feels like magic. You wonder how anyone ever survived writing raw SQL queries.
Then your app grows. You deploy to production. You open your monitoring tools a few weeks later, and the reality hits:

• Your AWS Lambda or Vercel serverless cold starts are now around 1.5 to 2 seconds.

• Your database CPU spikes to 90% during peak traffic because a nested include statement executed a big, un-indexed query chain behind your back.

• The Node process wastes 200MB+ of RAM at idle because of the deployment package’s bundled Rust binary.
This is the classic Prisma experience: legendary Developer Experience (DX) on day one, followed by silent performance bottlenecks in production on day 30.
Here is why developers are tired of the “magic” abstraction — and why Drizzle ORM is rapidly becoming the new standard for modern Node.js backends.
1. The Secret: Prisma’s Rust Engine
To understand why Prisma can feel sluggish in production, you have to look under the hood.
Prisma is not just a lightweight JavaScript library. When you install Prisma, it ships with a compiled Rust Query Engine Binary. When your Node.js application runs a query, it doesn’t just send a command to PostgreSQL or MySQL — it passes the query over an internal Inter-Process Communication (IPC) layer to this Rust binary, which translates your JS object into SQL, executes it, translates the SQL result back into Rust, and then serializes it back into JavaScript objects.
This architecture was designed to make query building consistent across multiple programming languages. But in a Node.js ecosystem dominated by serverless functions and edge computing, shipping a heavy native binary is a massive toll:

• Cold Start Penalties: Loading a native binary into memory on every serverless execution adds a good amount of latency.

• Memory Footprint: Running a separate engine binary inflates your container’s memory usage before you’ve even processed your first HTTP request.

• Edge Incompatibility: You can’t natively run heavy binaries on lightweight edge runtimes like Cloudflare Workers without complex proxy drivers.
2. The Problem with the Super Clean Code
Prisma makes fetching relational data really easy. Need a user, their posts, and the comments on those posts? You write this:
// Look how clean this is!
const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({
where: { id: 1 },
include: {
posts: {
include: {
comments: true,
},
},
},
});It looks innocent. But because Prisma hides the underlying SQL, it is easy to forget what this actually forces the database to do.

Depending on your Prisma version and database adapter, this nested include can either fire off multiple separate round-trip queries to the database or generate a massive SQL JOIN that returns thousands of duplicate row fields over the wire—leaving your Node.js process to do the heavy lifting of deduplicating and stitching that JSON back together in RAM.
Ignoring database mechanics always leads to performance bottlenecks down the road.
3. Drizzle ORM: SQL-First & Type-Safe
The frustration with high-level ORM “magic” led to the rise of Drizzle ORM.
Drizzle’s philosophy is fundamentally different: If you know SQL, you already know Drizzle.
Instead of inventing a custom schema DSL (schema.prisma) and compiling a Rust engine, Drizzle is a zero-dependency, pure TypeScript query builder. What you write in TypeScript maps 1:1 to the SQL query that gets executed.
How Drizzle Looks in Code:
import { db } from './db';
import { users, posts } from './schema';
import { eq } from 'drizzle-orm';const result = await db
.select({
userId: users.id,
userName: users.name,
postTitle: posts.title,
})
.from(users)
.leftJoin(posts, eq(users.id, posts.authorId))
.where(eq(users.id, 1));
Notice the difference:

• No Magic Engine: Drizzle is just a thin JavaScript wrapper around standard node database drivers (pg, mysql2, libsql).

• Predictable Performance: There is no binary, no IPC overhead, and zero query translation lag. The query you write is the exact SQL sent to the database.

• Instant Startup: Cold starts drop from seconds to single-digit milliseconds. It works natively anywhere: AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, Bun, or standard Node containers.
Prisma vs. Drizzle

Which One Should You Use?
This doesn’t mean Prisma is trash. Prisma pioneered modern developer experience in the Node ecosystem, and for specific use cases, it still shines:

• Use Prisma if: You are building rapid prototypes, internal admin tools, or small-scale monoliths where query performance isn’t a bottleneck and Prisma does not automatically create database indexes on foreign key fields. Studies analyzing production Prisma repositories found that over 55% of foreign keys were missing indexes, triggering a massive 150x performance penalty due to silent full table scans.

• Use Drizzle if: You are building production APIs, serverless microservices, edge applications, or high-throughput backends where database query optimization, memory usage, and sub-millisecond execution times actually matter.

We eventually realize that hiding SQL entirely is a leaky abstraction. Drizzle gives us the exact middle ground we’ve wanted: full control over our database queries, without giving up a single ounce of TypeScript safety.
